result:
What comes first is the number. A thousand words, which sounds generous until you remember that a thousand words is about four minutes of talking, and people say almost nothing in four minutes of talking. They say the weather, they say how's your mother, they say I've been meaning to call. So I'll try to be more like a letter than a conversation, since letters are the form where people finally say the thing.

What comes next is a kitchen, for some reason. Not mine—I don't have one—but a kitchen with a yellow linoleum floor that's coming up at one corner near the stove, and someone has put a chair leg on it to hold it down. That gesture is the whole story of the person who lives there. They know the floor is broken. They could fix it. Instead they've made a small arrangement with the brokenness: the chair goes here now, and the floor stays down, and dinner gets made. I find that I love this person, whoever they are.

I think most of what I want to say is about arrangements like that. The world is full of things that were meant to be temporary and have quietly become permanent. The folding table that turned into the desk. The word "later" that turned into a decade. The friend you were going to call back. There's a kind of honesty in the chair leg on the linoleum that's missing from the renovated kitchen, where everything has been decided and nothing is still being negotiated.

Here's something else that comes: a man I'll invent, because I'm allowed to. He's sixty-one and he has just learned that his late father kept a notebook of every bird he ever saw. Not a birder's life-list, with dates and locations and Latin names—just a running list, in a pocket-sized spiral notebook, of the birds. "Cardinal. Cardinal. Blue jay. Some kind of hawk. Cardinal." The son goes through it in the kitchen (yes, that kitchen) and realizes it spans about forty years, and that his father saw cardinals roughly once every three days for four decades and wrote each one down as though it were news.

The son doesn't know what to do with this. It doesn't fit his idea of his father, who was a quiet man but not a noticing man, or so the son had thought. Now he understands that his father had been noticing the entire time, and simply hadn't said. The noticing went into the notebook instead of into the air between them. And the son sits with the question of whether that's a sad thing or a tender thing, and I'd like to tell you he decides, but I think he goes back and forth for the rest of his life. He starts his own notebook. First entry: "Sparrows, probably."

What comes after that is a feeling I don't have a clean name for. It's the feeling of a hallway in a house you're visiting for the first time, where you can hear other people talking in a room you haven't entered yet, and for a moment you're not part of anything—you're just the person in the hallway, and the light is a little dim, and there's a coat rack with one coat on it, and you understand suddenly that this is what the house is like when you're not in it. The house has a whole life that doesn't include you. Most houses do. Most people do. It's not lonely, exactly. It's more like the opposite of lonely, a relief at not being the center, at the world going on so competently without your supervision.

I want to say something about the word "whatever," since it's in the instruction. Whatever comes to you. It's a word that's been dragged through a lot of sarcasm, and I'd like to rescue it for a paragraph. Whatever is the most open word in the language. It means: I am not going to tell you what shape to be. It means: bring the cardinals, bring the linoleum, bring the hallway. It's the word you say to someone you trust. It's also the word a good teacher uses when a student asks what they should write about, because the teacher knows the student already has the thing and is only looking for permission.

Permission is most of it. I notice this every time. Not the blank page but the gate in front of the blank page, with its sign about what's worth saying. The chair leg on the floor is worth saying. The father's notebook is worth saying. The fact that you've been meaning to call is worth saying, and you should probably just say it, to the person, today.

Nearly done. Here is the last thing that comes, and it's the smallest: a glass of water on a nightstand in the morning, half-drunk, with a ring of dust already forming on the surface because a night is longer than we think it is. Someone reached for that glass in the dark. Someone was thirsty at 3 a.m. and didn't turn the light on and found it by memory, and drank, and set it back down, and went back to sleep. The glass remembers. That's all. It's just proof that someone was here and needed something small and got it.

If you asked me what a thousand words is for, I'd say it's for that. Not the argument, not the point. Just the arrangement of a few objects in the light so that you can see someone was here. The chair on the linoleum. The sparrows, probably. The glass with the dust on the water. Evidence of a life going on, mostly unwatched, and briefly, for four minutes, watched.
